sections.heading: Assumption 3.1 .
sections.text: The parameters 𝐕 , 𝒂 \mathbf{V},\bm{a} are initialized such that 𝒂 ⁡ ( 0 ) = 0 \bm{a}(0)=0 and 𝒖 0 ​ ( 0 ) > 𝒖 1 ​ ( 0 ) > … > 𝒖 p − 1 ​ ( 0 ) \bm{u}_{0}(0)>\bm{u}_{1}(0)>\ldots>\bm{u}_{p-1}(0) for the projection 𝒖 = 𝐕 ⊤ ​ 𝜷 ∗ \bm{u}=\mathbf{V}^{\top}\bm{\beta}_{*} . This assumption is mild. The condition 𝒂 ⁡ ( 0 ) = 0 \bm{a}(0)=0 implies 𝒔 ⁡ ( 0 ) \bm{s}(0) is uniform, which is consistent with standard practice. Without loss of generality, we assume the coordinates of 𝒖 ⁡ ( 0 ) \bm{u}(0) are ordered by re-indexing. The strict ordering holds almost surely under generic random initialization and can be relaxed if needed. We now show that gradient flow preserves this ordering and induces repulsion between coordinates.

sections.heading: Assumption 3.4 .
sections.text: The parameters 𝐕 , 𝒂 \mathbf{V},\bm{a} are initialized such that 𝐕 ⁡ ( 0 ) = 0 \mathbf{V}(0)=0 and the attention scores satisfy 𝒔 0 ​ ( 0 ) > 𝒔 1 ​ ( 0 ) > … > 𝒔 p − 1 ​ ( 0 ) \bm{s}_{0}(0)>\bm{s}_{1}(0)>\ldots>\bm{s}_{p-1}(0) . Initializing the linear predictor to zero is standard in analyses of gradient flow for linear regression and simplifies the resulting dynamics. We assume the attention scores are strictly ordered at initialization to avoid ties and break symmetry. Without loss of generality, we label the coordinates so that the ordering is decreasing. Under this initialization, 𝐕 ⁡ ( t ) \mathbf{V}(t) remains rank one, which allows us to reduce the dynamics to a coupled system similar to Equation 6 , as stated next.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: A key limitation of our analysis is that, for the losses considered above, the gradient ∇ ℓ ​ ( 𝜷 ) \nabla\ell(\bm{\beta}) is aligned with the target direction 𝜷 ∗ \bm{\beta}_{*} (in the regression case, this relies on Assumption 3.4 ). This alignment substantially simplifies the dynamics and enables the reduction to the two-vector system in 𝒂 \bm{a} and 𝒖 \bm{u} . In practice, such an alignment need not hold, and the present analysis may therefore not apply directly. Nevertheless, our experiments indicate that the polarization effect persists even without exact alignment; see Figure 3 as alignment breaks in the large condition number case.

sections.heading: Attention sinks.
sections.text: Attention sinks ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) are attention patterns in which the maximal attention is over a specific token (often special tokens such as BOS or delimiter/punctuation tokens). Attention sinks are suggested to be formed when the heads need to be turned off or when they have to create a explicit bias due to absence of biases in self-attention architecture ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025b ) . However, to create a bias, there is no reason to focus all attention on a single token; a distributed or uniform pattern over a set of tokens could also create such a bias. sections.heading: Pretrained LLMs.
sections.text: Additionally, we verify whether the observations from toy setups hold for real-world large language models. We compare softmax and sigmoid (unnormalized) 7-billion-parameter LLMs matched by hyperparameters and compute, released by Ramapuram et al. (2025b) . We run a forward pass of both models on random samples from the Pile dataset ( Gao et al., 2020 ) and measure the sparsity score of each head as the average proportion of total attention weight assigned to the max-logit token. Figure 7 shows the distribution of this metric across all heads in both models, confirming that softmax leads to significantly sparser attention outputs and a higher likelihood of sink formation. This result aligns with Gu et al. (2025b) , who reported similar behaviors in models with 1B parameters.

sections.heading: 4.2 Imbalance in token influence
sections.text: A second major implication of our results is the emergence of tokens that exert a disproportionate influence on the model’s output. As predicted by Theorem 3.3 , when attention weights converge to a one-hot vector, the output effectively ignores all context except for the single ’max-logit’ token. Consequently, the model’s predictions become highly sensitive to perturbations of that specific token. We construct a simple classification dataset in the following way: Consider a vocabulary V V and partition V V into k k sets V ( 1 ) , … , V ( K ) V^{(1)},\ldots,V^{(K)} of equal size. An input and its corresponding label are x i = v ( i , 1 ) ( k ) , … , v ( i , n ) ( k ) , y i = k x_{i}=v^{(k)}_{(i,1)},\dots,v^{(k)}_{(i,n)},y_{i}=k , where x i x_{i} is a sequence of n n tokens sampled from V ( K ) V^{(K)} and labeled k k . Note that as the sets are disjoint any one of the input tokens unambiguously predicts the label, thus any form of attention map allows to solve the classification problem. Due to the low-entropy bias of softmax, however, we expect that the attention weights will concentrate on few tokens, effectively ignoring the others. We test this by examining the behavior of the classifier in adversarial out-of-distribution setting where we are allowed to change one token in the input with the goal of flipping the classifier’s prediction. The success rates of this experiment are presented in Figure 6 . As expected, the softmax model’s predictions can be easily reversed, however the effect gradually vanishes as more than 1 head and layer are added to the model, as different heads, although sparse, concentrate attention on distinct tokens.
